# vendor

gpui-kit's code editor, forked so it can be made fast enough for large files (measured by `koyo-rs/koyo-bench`).

| Directory | Crate | Version | Upstream |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gpui-base/` | `gpui-base` | 0.8.1 | [longbridge/gpui-kit](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit) `crates/base` at `99576db58ec8103417c41a092e891b4022d24e7e` |
| `gpui-component/` | `gpui-component` | 0.8.1 | [longbridge/gpui-kit](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit) `crates/component` at the same commit |
| `gpui-fast-apple/` | `gpui-fast-apple` | 0.1.12 | the crates.io package, unpacked from the `.crate` whose checksum `Cargo.lock` holds |
| `gpui-fast-macos/` | `gpui-fast-macos` | 0.1.12 | the crates.io package ([longbridge/gpui-fast](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-fast)), unpacked the same way |

Both started as the crates.io packages unpacked as they are, `Cargo.toml` (as normalized by crates.io), `Cargo.toml.orig`, `Cargo.lock`, `.cargo_vcs_info.json` and `LICENSE-APACHE` included; each `.crate` matched the checksum in the workspace's `Cargo.lock` before it was unpacked. `git log -- koyo-rs/vendor/` shows what has changed since.

The workspace's `Cargo.toml` (`koyo-rs/Cargo.toml`) puts them in place of the registry crates with `[patch.crates-io]`. The `gpui-kit` facade still comes from crates.io and re-exports both, so the build holds one copy of each: `cargo tree -i gpui-base` names `vendor/gpui-base`.

Neither crate is a workspace member. They keep upstream's code style and their own `[lints]` table; the workspace lint policy and `script/hygiene` cover the `koyo-rs/koyo*` crates only. Being path dependencies, their warnings aren't capped as a registry crate's are: `script/lint` holds them to rustc's and Clippy's defaults with every warning an error.

All four are licensed Apache-2.0, as is this repository; their license files (`LICENSE-APACHE`, `LICENSE`) stay with them.

## gpui-fast-apple

GPUI's Metal renderer, vendored for two changes, marked `Koyo:` in `src/metal_renderer.rs`, `src/shaders.metal`, `src/fast/rounded_clip_shader.rs` and `src/fast/composition.rs`. The first: it draws a BGRA surface in the window's own frame: a simulator's or the agent desktop's picture, in the surface its host shares with the app (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/surfaces.rs`). A browser page's frame came the same way until pages became native views (`docs/native-pages.md`); what was only a page's, a picture smaller than its surface (`set_surface_picture`), has no caller now and is still in the renderer. Upstream draws only biplanar video surfaces. `metal_renderer::set_surface_picture` says how much of the shared surface, from its top left, is the page; that part goes over the surface's bounds, and the rest of its content mask is filled by the picture's edge pixels reaching out, as while a page is laid out a frame behind a pane that grew. Rounded clips apply to it as to GPUI's other primitives. A page surface's Metal texture is made over its `IOSurface` directly, not through Core Video's texture cache, which keeps a pixel buffer until the cache is flushed; each frame keeps the pixel buffers and textures of the page surfaces it samples until the GPU has finished it (a pixel buffer marks its surface in use while it lives, which the browser host reads before painting into a surface), and no longer. Drawn with everything round it, the page can't reach the screen a frame apart from the pane's edge, which a page in a layer of its own did unless GPUI presented in Core Animation's transaction, at the cost of the window's frame rate. `build.rs` also allows the unused `stage` its shader helper module has when shaders aren't compiled ahead of time, as a path dependency's warnings aren't capped.

The second: it takes a picture of part of a frame, for the tab switcher's cards (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/shell/pictures.rs`, `docs/tab-switcher.md` 4). `metal_renderer::set_surface_capture` marks a BGRA pixel buffer as one a picture is taken into. Painted in a scene, such a buffer draws nothing; once the frame is drawn, `MetalRenderer::take_pictures` copies the frame's pixels under the buffer's bounds, as far as its content mask shows them, into a texture with mips, and draws that, shrunk, into the buffer's own `IOSurface` with the page surfaces' pipeline, whose sampler reads the mips for it (`shaders.metal`). Another buffer over the same surface then paints as any BGRA surface. A picture is taken at most every quarter second while the buffer's request stays the same, and with the next frame when it changes. Only a surface painted in the frame's own scene has its picture taken, not one inside a layer's content. A window's frames can't be read while its layer is display-only (`framebufferOnly`), which upstream leaves it outside test builds: the first picture asked of a window turns that off for each of its layers, and is taken from the next frame.

A window that composes native views draws in layers, each a frame of its own with a renderer of its own (`src/fast/composition.rs`), and a picture is of all of them. The lowest layer's renderer takes it as above; the renderer of a layer over it (`MetalRenderer::draws_over`) then draws its own part of the frame over that picture, once for each the lowest takes. The layers' renderers share what they keep of the window's pictures, the last one taken and the texture a part of a frame is copied into, and one command queue, so the GPU draws the upper part after the lower. The native views themselves are in no frame: `metal_renderer::set_surface_pane` marks a BGRA buffer as a pane, which draws nothing in a scene and which the renderer of an upper layer fills in a picture, rounded, under its own part. Koyo's native surfaces can paint one over themselves, as its Liquid Glass does (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/native/surface.rs`). One attachment says what a surface is, a page's picture, one a picture is taken into or a pane (`Mark`), so drawing a surface reads it once.

## gpui-fast-macos

GPUI's macOS windows, vendored for changes marked `Koyo:` in `src/fast/composition.rs`, `src/window.rs` and `src/responders.rs`, each for a window that composes native views (`docs/native-pages.md` 6):

- Whose a mouse button's events are (`send_window_event`). Upstream gave each drag move to whatever lay under the pointer, and kept one native view as the owner of every button until it had counted each button's release. A drag pressed on GPUI's own content, a divider beside a browser page, lost the moves made over the page; and a release the window never saw (a menu the press opened had tracked it, a drag session had taken it) left that view the owner for good, every later drag of any button going to it. Here a press owns its button: the view that took a button's press, by the button's number, gets that button's drag and release wherever the pointer is by then, a button whose press GPUI took has no entry and its events go GPUI's way, each press says anew whose its button is, and a view that leaves the window holds no press.
- A release GPUI never hears (`lost_releases`). GPUI's core holds a press over a native view as that view's until it hears the release, and meanwhile no press reaches GPUI's own content. GPUI's view keeps the presses it passed on and, once a move with no button down or a press while the hand's button for one is up says a press is over, tells GPUI of its release first.
- The modifiers (`send_window_event`, `route_keys`). A flags-changed event goes to GPUI's view as well whenever another view, a page's, has the keyboard: GPUI hears the modifiers only through its own view, and ⌃ let go after ⌃⇥ in a page never reached the tab switcher. GPUI already counts a change it hears twice once.
- The app's say over the keyboard (`src/responders.rs`, `docs/keyboard.md`). The app gives the windows a `Responders` (`set_responders`), which each of GPUI's windows and panels tells, on the main thread: every change of its first responder, whoever made it (`makeFirstResponder:`, overridden on both window classes, calls `AppKit`'s own and then tells the change); every key going down or up before the window delivers it to its first responder (`route_keys`, in `send_window_event`: key equivalents have been offered by then, by the application, and aren't touched); and every press of a mouse button before it's handed on, with the view under the pointer when it's in a native view of the composition (from the hit test `send_window_event` makes anyway) or nil for GPUI's own content (`tell_press`). Upstream has none of it: a native view that took the first responder on its own, as a browser page does as it opens, kept every key with GPUI never hearing of it. With no `Responders` given, the windows behave as upstream's, but for the other changes here.
- One key, one owner (`src/responders.rs`, `Offers`; `handle_key_event`; `route_keys`, `offer_first`). A key equivalent can be offered to GPUI's view three times over: by `AppKit`'s own pass, by the window's key routing (`offer_first` offers a ⌘ or ⌃ key going down to GPUI's view before delivering it whenever another view has the keyboard, as `AppKit` makes no pass of its own while the app isn't in front), and handed back by a page that left it (the browser host's `unhandled_key`). GPUI's view dispatches it once at most, matched by the event's time: on its first offer if the app says GPUI comes first (`Responders::gpui_first`: Koyo keeps its tab and window keys, and leaves every other key to a page that has the keyboard first), else once the page hands it back. Without it, a page saw a key GPUI took as well: on the agent desktop a ⌘L opened Koyo's address and reached the page.
- A made-up release is logged (`lost_releases`): one line at `koyo::input` for each release GPUI is told of that it never heard, naming the button only.
- A key equivalent matched by its event (`handle_key_event`). Upstream lets a key press go by when it's the same keystroke as the last key equivalent, which AppKit sends first for some keys; a key a page leaves comes to GPUI as a key equivalent with no key press after it, and the next same key typed in GPUI was lost. The two are matched by the event's time too.
